speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the economic statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) brought cuts to the industrial support program under Regional and Industrial Development even far more reaching than many at first realized. Such an action has amounted to withdrawing large amounts of direct investment by the Government in industrial development, job creation, and the economic development of less affluent Canadian regions affecting, in particular, small community Canada.
Regional development grants represent direct assistance for the location of new industries in various regions where industrial development lags behind the primary industrial zones of southern Ontario and Montreal. The grants represent an opportunity for communities in all parts of Canada to participate in the development of Canada's economic potential. Such grants help to reduce regional disparity and make all Canadians feel part of the real nation.
Admittedly, regions receiving industrial development grants do not represent areas of economic power and influence, nor do they represent political numbers in Parliament. That is an important reason why industrial development efforts must be maintained in all regions of Canada.
The cold-hearted cuts to regional industrial development funding exposes the heartlessness of the Conservative Government and its new policy. The Government promised tens of thousands of jobs the day after it was elected. The law of the jungle is at work. The Government's new political philosophy is to let the strong survive.
I regret to inform the Hon. Member his time has expired.

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE CONSEQUENCES OF ESTABLISHING CANADIAN UNION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all Canadians concerned with economic recovery and full employment must be impressed by the implications of the separation of the Canadian section of the United Auto Workers from its American parent union. The possibility of this union's reorganization adversely affecting the Canadian auto industry has become clear. Already spokesmen for major auto makers are indicating it could encourage a reshaping of their corporate structures. This could mean possible changes in the role of Canadian plants in their production plans.
The auto industry's extraordinary recovery since August, 1982 has been a major reason for the measure of recovery Canada has enjoyed, especially in Ontario. In the constituency of Scarborough West, for example, the auto plant of General Motors employs 2,500 people. Any factor that can mean a production cut, or a plant closure, must be seen as a major threat to our economy. Government, management, and labour need the fullest co-operation to make sure internal re-organization plans in the industry do not threaten the livelihoods of many thousands.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Members of this House and all Canadians must be very happy about the speech made by the Right Hon. Prime Minister before the New York Economic Club. The Prime Minister's words were received with enthusiasm by the financial and industrial elite of the United States. I was particularly pleased with the reference to Quebec which provides excellent opportunities for foreign investment and is getting in step with the broad movement towards national reconciliation undertaken by our Government.
Mr. Speaker, it was an historic moment on the evening of December 10, putting an end to twenty years of confrontation, twenty years of coldly sterile relations under the previous Liberal administration.

subsubtopic: IMPACT OF BUDGETARY CUT-BACKS ON PERSONNEL AND PROGRAMMING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday was a black day for the more than 1,100 employees of the CBC who now face early retirement or lay-offs due to the knife-wielding approach of the new Government to the federal budget. These people represent the direct human cost of the actions of an insensitive Government. The inability of the CBC to undertake the development and production of new dramas, children's programs, and informational programs which have gained international renown, is a cruel cut to Canada's cultural and social development.
The CBC is a national institution. It has an ongoing role to play in the development of Canada's national identity and in strengthening national unity through communication. The budget cuts imposed by the Government demonstrate the ignorance of the new Government in recognizing that sometimes there are costs which simply must be borne by a Government if we are, as Canadians, to have a nation. The CBC is one of those costs. Canada, and Canadianism, are not
a commodity. Unfortunately, that is how the new Government sees Canada.
The budgetary cuts inflicted by the Conservative Government will lead to an even greater cost in lost cultural development and communication among Canadians in all regions for years to come.

subsubtopic: REDUCTION OF SERVICES IN RURAL REGIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring a vast inequity to the attention of the House. While urban Canadians enjoy the luxury of daily mail delivery to their doors and are usually able to purchase postal services such as money orders, registered letters, and special delivery, within a five or 10 minute drive, rural Canadians are having their services reduced, or even cancelled, and must travel as far as 30 miles to reach the nearest post office.
In the meantime the President of Canada Post has made several speeches lauding his success in reducing the corporation's deficit and in meeting the objective of improving service. The deficit may be reduced, but I think the President is sorely mistaken if he believes that there is a renewed consumer confidence, as he puts it.
Since my election to Parliament just a few months ago, 1 have been contacted by an alarming number of constituents from my riding in rural Manitoba. So far, five separate cases have been brought to my attention where postal service has either been reduced or eliminated altogether. The residents of these small rural communities feel that they are paying the price of Canada Post's program of restraint.
I would suggest that the President of Canada Post should take a second look at his level of customer confidence, especially in rural areas, because I firmly believe that Canada Post's deficit reduction program is being borne on the backs of rural Canadians.

subsubtopic: LIBERAL PARTY'S POLICY ON NUCLEAR ARMAMENT FREEZE PROPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to call the attention of the House to the verbal gymnastics and contradictions which attend the question of where the Liberal Party caucus stands on the nuclear freeze proposal. The Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien) says that there has been a change in policy. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) will not confirm that there has been a change in policy. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) says that they have a different position
December 12, 1984

now because they are in opposition, thus admitting the moral bankruptcy of Liberal politics.
The fact of the matter is that the Liberals have not changed their policy on the nuclear freeze. They went out of their way the other day to make an amendment to our motion so that they could appear to be for the nuclear freeze by removing from the motion that which would have made it a concrete recommendation. The Liberals are still against the nuclear freeze, and people who support the nuclear freeze should have their heads examined if they believe otherwise.

Mr. Speaker, the previous Government did not put enough emphasis on this international event which is aimed at giving young people a say and a share in the economic, social and political life of our society. How could we forget that the previous Government always neglected young people, that it has done nothing to reduce unemployment or support training programs for, and projects by, Canadian youth?
Mr. Speaker, we must condemn the previous Government's lack of consistency in its youth policies and programs. I would therefore urge our Government to try as much as possible to correct the mistakes made by the previous Government by extending the expiry dates of certain special grant programs provided within the framework of International Youth Year.

subsubtopic: CLOSURE OF GANDER, NFLD., RADIO STATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the CBC cuts announced yesterday as a result of the policy of the Government are emasculating the corporation.
It is not the high profile national news identity that forms the raison d'etre for this corporation. It is its promotion and encouragement of cultural identity and opportunities for Canadians in the local things done at each CBC outlet that make this corporation worth-while.
The CBC has announced the closing of Radio Station CGB in Gander, Newfoundland, one of its first stations in the province. It has the highest area ratings in listening audience
of any CBC radio station in Canada. This announced closing is uncalled for, and makes no economic sense at all.
I am asking the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) to use the authority given to him under the Broadcasting Act to reverse that decision. The Government, in forcing the CBC to cut, has handed it not a paring knife but a chain-saw.
During the election campaign we heard from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) a kind of inverted snobbery toward the CBC, to pooh-pooh everything the CBC does. This should not be allowed to translate into irrational and cruel actions such as the closing of CGB Gander.
Blinded by the deficit, the Government is crippling the people, crippling the environment, crippling the economy, and now it is crippling our cultural heritage.

Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that more and more Canadians are greatly concerned about the size of our national debt. Although the official debt has been expressed at some $190 billion, this amount does not include the accumulated debt of all the federal Crown corporations, some $60 billion. It does not include some $50 billion collected by the Government in contributions made to the Canada Pension Plan, the Public Service Superannuation Pension Fund, the Armed Forces Pension Fund, and the RCMP Pension Fund. The money collected in pension contributions goes into general revenue and is spent by Governments to pay current bills.
[DOT] (MIS)
All in all, Mr. Speaker, our national debt in reality is some $300 billion.
This is the unfortunate legacy that our Government has inherited from the former Government.
This huge debt is one reason why all Canadians have been asked to bite the bullet, and for each and every one of us to sacrifice and work together in an unselfish way to get Canada out of the economic mire and back on track again to full employment and economic growth.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is imperative that we make every effort now to make the necessary changes and the necessary sacrifices to curb this debt if Canada is to survive.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am fairly confident at this time that Hon. Members are familiar with the intent of Bill C-5. In a nutshell, it is an amendment to the Freshwater Fish Marketing Act to increase the permitted borrowing limit from the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation to $30 million from the present borrowing ceiling of $20 million which was set 10 years ago. In the fishing industry, as is the case in most businesses over the last 10 years, market prices have risen along with operating costs, the cost of fuels, wages and so on. This certainly holds true with the FFMC which has seen its operating budget escalating steadily.
A recently prepared five-year plan of the Corporation shows that its working capital and fixed assets requirements will exceed $20 million in the fiscal year 1985-86, and within a year will be in the region of $24 million. It is significant that the initial payment of the Corporation, that is the amount of money paid out to the 3,500 fishermen in the FFMC area at the start of the season, based on predicted market prices, has risen from a total of $9 million in 1974 to more than $20 million in 1983. As Hon. Members may have noticed from a recent press release, total sales of the Corporation in 1983-84 were in excess of $44 million, which is a record amount.
Perhaps we should point out that the FFMC draws its working capital through loans from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). It is, of course, not allowed to borrow more from that or any other source than that set out in the Act as its permitted borrowing limit.
Another point I would like to stress is that under the Corporation's mandate it is obliged to purchase all the fish offered to it by the fishermen who operate in the five million square kilometers of territory comprising the area covered by the FFMC. Most of these fishermen are native people who, in most instances, have no alternative means of making a living. It would be most unfortunate if these hardworking Canadian citizens had to suffer as a result of the FFMC having insufficient working capital. That situation could easily arise in the coming year if the credit ceiling is not raised as proposed in this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be brief. There is some urgency to pass this Bill today. We on this side of the House certainly agree with Bill
C-5 because there are 3,500 fishermen, many of whom are native fishermen, who require this borrowing authority increase.
This Bill was previously introduced by the Government of which I was a member back in 1980. I recall that the Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) did not have many favourable comments about this corporation during second reading stage of this Bill. He felt that it was extremely monopolistic in regard to the private sector in that part of the region. He went on to say that he supported the Bill because he is a good Party supporter, but I think the Hon. Member's remarks might give us cause to believe there is something in the Bill that we did not understand.
Although I am reluctant to bring that up, I would suggest to the Minister, the Parliamentary Secretary and the Committee on Fisheries and Forestry that witnesses should appear on behalf of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Agency so that we can delve into those accusations a little further.
I am extremely pleased to see the progress of the corporation this year. A recent news release on December 6 stated that there would be a final payment for 1983-84 amounting to almost $6 million, of which the single highest pay-out to an individual fisherman was $78,000. That fact reflects what we have thought about the corporation over the years. However, due to the reservations expressed by the Hon. Member for Western Arctic, we should question witnesses from the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation in the committee to see if there is any justice to those accusations.
There are no more speakers from the Official Opposition and we are prepared to see this Bill passed as soon as possible.

As I said at second reading, the problem is that the FFMC enjoys a monopoly. No one else is allowed in that business. The fishermen cannot sell their products to anyone other than the Crown corporation FFMC. In return, as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Gass) pointed out, FFMC is obligated to take all the fish that the fishermen make available to them. However, there is nothing mentioned about the price that it has to pay. Therefore it can say that it will take the fish but only pay five cents a pound for it. The provision in the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation Act which states that, in return for granting FFMC a monopoly, it must take the fish really does not make sense. There is an easy way for FFMC to avoid that.
Those who have studied this matter independently have found that in all probability alternative methods of fish marketing could be established. People could go into that business, buy fish from the fishermen and take it across interprovincial and international boundaries in order to develop markets for that fish for the existing species that are marketed and for species that are underutilized or not utilized at all.
If the monopoly was revoked, I believe the enterprise within people would work wonders for the fishermen. It has and continues to be the policy of the Progressive Conservative Party that Crown corporations such as the FFMC should not enjoy that monopoly. This was well thought out prior to the last election campaign. It was an election promise made to fishermen in freshwater country that when we took over the reins of government that monopoly would be revoked.
This issue must not be allowed to go to the bottom of the heap. Perhaps it is not a great national issue involving all of Canada but it is certainly important in certain areas of the Prairies and certainly in the Northwest Territories. We owe it to those fishermen to carry out our election promise.

Apparently, the reason for that delay is that the Conservatives are divided on their own Bill. I find that quite extraordinary. Bill C-5 is one of its first Bills and the Government is already divided among itself in its large caucus.
I listened carefully to what the Member for Western Arctic said. He aroused memories I have of seeing fish coming out of the water at the north end of Great Slave Lake at this time of the year when I lived up there approximately ten years ago. I remember how important it is to the people. It is very interesting to see that when the fish come out of the water they freeze instantly. You do not have the problem of putting them into anything; the temperature is so cold that it instantly freezes them.
There are some problems with what the Hon. Member for Western Arctic said. As I understood what he said, he objects, and his Party objected in the campaign-but not as it brings the Bill into the House-to a monopoly situation. I am confused about this, Mr. Speaker. How far would the Member go? Would he get rid of the Canadian Wheat Board? That is a monopoly marketing organization, is it not? Does the Hon. Member believe in orderly marketing? The concept of orderly marketing was to try and give the producer a decent value for his product.
Maximum return.

As my colleague has said, the maximum return for the product. We have great experience on that in Canada. We fought those battles 30 or 40 years ago. In the so-called free market, which turned out to be not so free, producer kept undercutting producer and the prices would go down and down and down. Does the Hon. Member honestly believe that if this were a free market for fish or for selling to a private buyer that the fishermen would have any more control over the fish? I am not so sure they would. I think they might be better off with a freshwater fish marketing board.
I accept the fact that the Hon. Member represents and speaks for his area. Obviously he is reflecting problems of the fishermen in his area, in the Arctic, an area which I have already said I appreciate and love a great deal. If they are having problems, perhaps we should have a further look at this situation in committee. The Hon. Member said the Bill was railroaded through the committee. To use his words, "it was a railroad job". I remind the Hon. Member that he is a member of the governing Party. The Conservatives control the committees. I hope he would have a little more influence with his own Government not to have a Bill railroaded through the committee. If there is a problem, it seems to me the committee should have another look.
The Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) had a quite genuine suggestion, and I would be prepared to go along with

what he said. I do not think it is in this Bill. This is a minor Bill in the sense that it just increases the credit ceiling so that the marketing board would have adequate working capital. Now is not the time to do it but the Member has flagged the problem.
I am not sure I agree with him. I think there are problems when you start departing from orderly marketing from the experience we have had in Canada. I would remind the Hon. Member that the reason the freshwater fish marketing board was set up-and I remind his colleagues too-is because the private sector failed. The fishermen were in desperate need. Member's colleagues, in their great ideological pursuit of the holy grail of private enterprise at all costs, should give pause, as my friend from Calgary should give pause, and ask themselves why was this thing set up. The House resumed Tuesday, December 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Stevens that Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development.

Mr. Speaker, when we concluded debate on this Bill yesterday afternoon at five o'clock, I was just about to open the question of benefits for foreign investment. That seems to me to be the crucial question that should be considered. I suggested in passing that the Government was bringing this Bill in with much of the Christmas spirit about it. Santa Claus will bring us good things if only we are good. We will throw the door open and foreign investment will come in and all sorts of good things will happen. It is precisely the question whether good things will follow from foreign investment which deserves to be considered.
I suggested also that proponents of foreign investment have never, in my opinion, subjected the process and its consequences to the sort of consideration that it deserves to have. That for governments is particularly serious because they have the means of clarifying the matter. One can to some extent in
a theoretical way open up the question and consider what some of the consequences are. That is what I want to do for a few minutes today.
First, there is concern about the need for capital in this country. It is probably not all that difficult an exercise to suggest gargantuan totals of capital being needed between now and 1990. The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) suggested one of those totals. At the same time we are told that Canadians save at a world-leading rate. Given the levels of saving that occur here, one would not think the need for capital was actually as inordinate as is being suggested by the Government in bringing this Bill before us. One might recognize that when foreign investment is encouraged and when very large parts of the economic activity that occur in a country is foreign controlled, in Canadian manufacturing particularly and in large areas of resource extraction-it is overwhelmingly the case that so much of the activity is carried out in companies owned by people outside of Canada-the result year by year is an outflow of capital from Canada. There is no net gain at all.
When Government does not recognize that kind of reality, one begins to suspect it is being ideological and downright irresponsible in the economic policy which it puts before the country. On the score of capital for Canada, foreign investment can be an incredibly short-sighted gain. There are some other areas that are so enormously important to the economic development of this country. Surely what people mean when they talk about capital is technology, the bringing in to the country of knowledge presently not available. When we think of that kind of question and its ramifications, we have even more reason to be concerned about turning to capital investment for a simple answer.
The reality of the matter is that having technology imported into the country by reason of foreign investment can be an incredibly expensive gift to any people. If technology were not available, it would not be the easiest thing in the world but what would happen to Canadians, to the scientists, engineers and people involved in adapting technology and applying it? Canadian research and development would have to be done in order to fill those gaps. When we depend on others to bring the technology into the country, we close doors to our engineers and scientists. We shut off employment opportunities. If Government is ultimately concerned about foreign investment in order to ensure employment, again we have an incredibly short-sighted action in depending upon others to do these things for us.
If we think of employment in higher levels of management, New Democrats do not usually worry about that very quickly, but in terms of development and leadership of the country it is important too. When we depend on foreign investment to provide the capital and the technology, we are likely to get the skills and the management direction with it as well. It is a subject of the most profound importance to a country to consider what happens to it when the leadership and the direction of its economic affairs is coming from persons outside the country and when it is not Canadians who have the
December 12, 1984

opportunity to benefit. A few able or very fortunate Canadians may rise through the international structure and be lost to Canada. At a time when skilled management leadership of the country should have opportunities to work here on a large scale, we lose them as a result of foreign investment.
We should think about another area of economic activity and ask ourselves what happens in trade areas as far as imports and exports are concerned. What are the possibilities of having more extensive processing of raw material in Canada? In the past we looked to raw material, together with foreign investment; foreign investment in Canadian resources was the basis for Canadian prosperity. What happens in the case of foreign investment? All too often companies are established in the country with only one purpose, that is, to extract the product and get it out to markets in their home countries. Over the years it has been sent to the United States, especially since the Second World War and farther back into this century. When it is between a subsidiary in Canada and a parent company in the United States, we know that the pricing which occurs means low returns in Canada and high profits in the United States. Income flows and the bases for capital are lost to Canada as a result of the establishment of subsidiaries in this country. We worry about imports, about Canada having such an incredibly high level of imports, particularly in manufactured goods. Opportunities are closed off. When we think of those things, we realize that it is American and other foreign subsidiaries which are overwhelmingly importers of manufactured goods.
On point after point I suggest that the Canadian economy suffers and employment opportunities are lost. The future of the country is blasted when we look to foreign investment. For those reasons I feel a deep anxiety about the Bill before us.
Once upon a time George Grant in Lament for a Nation talked about the Conservatives having a sense of the country's future. These days when debating Investment Canada, that becomes the fiction many of us felt for years that it was. Conservatives are betraying their heritage these days in bringing this legislation before Parliament and presuming to turn Canada in that direction.

I thank you for your courtesy, Mr. Speaker. I have followed the debate thus far with great interest. As we all know, this is perhaps the most important Bill to be put before the House before the Christmas recess. The Bill will attract the attention of Canadians in every region from coast to coast because of its far-reaching and long-term implications.
I listened yesterday to the intervention of the Minister who is sponsoring this Bill. Quite frankly, I admit that I was startled by some of his statements. As reported at page 1090 of Hansard, he said the following:
-what we are saying is that with respect to new investment, as most of the Members realize from the kits we distributed, there will be no review other than in a very narrow sector.
Will it be to the benefit of Canadians to have no review other than in a very narrow sector? For some years we have had the benefit of the FIRA process which has thoroughly taken into account the desirability of acting in the interests of Canadians. This has been done in a way which has steered foreign investment in a manner that would be beneficial to our own long-term interests. Negotiations took place with FIRA and foreign investors in order to achieve the highest possible benefits for Canadians.

December 12, 1984
Investment Canada Act
In making his statement evidently the Minister is giving up a very valuable and important review process which has served us well. In that sense he is abdicating an important role on the part of the Government of Canada on behalf of all Canadians.
The Bill as presented to us will not only have a very limited review in a narrow sector, but it will give the Minister total discretionary powers. It means that he will be the sole emperor who decides whether or not certain types of investment will be admitted into Canada. Therefore he will not have the benefit of consulting with Cabinet or his own caucus. He will make his decision in isolation without perhaps taking into account the interests of the minister of industry, trade and commerce or other Ministers who have regional concerns and may want to have a say in the nature, direction and timing of certain investments.
Also in yesterday's intervention he indicated that if the Minister had not made up his mind after 75 days, a particular application would be deemed to have been approved. I find that very difficult to believe; however I have read it in the Bill. It is in Clause 22(3). I see the Hon. Member leaving. If he would stay in his seat, he would learn something. The net effect of Clause 22(3) will be that the Minister may use it when he does not want to make an unfavourable decision; he could let the time period lapse and the matter would be resolved that way. Is that a sensible and responsible way to govern and to protect the interests of Canadian industries or Canadian small businesses? They may be affected by the lapsing provision in the Bill.
I also looked in the Bill to find any reference to Canadian interests because, as was indicated in Clause 2, its purpose is to encourage investment in Canada by Canadians and non-Canadians. Once one goes beyond Clause 2, where does one find a reference to Canadians in the Bill? The Bill is some 30 or 40 pages long. The only place I could find a reference to Canadians was under the duties of the Minister in Clause 5(b). The rest of the Bill makes reference to anything other than Canadian interests.
What is this Bill intended to do? If one looks at it in its totality, one cannot help but conclude, regretfully, that the Bill was conceived in isolation. It has been put forward without the benefit of an over-all industrial strategy. There is no provision to enhance research and development in Canada in order to enhance the capacity of our industry to expand, develop new products and, therefore, new markets and the creation of jobs.
There is no provision for the protection of our cultural identity and cultural industry for those Canadians who make their living in cultural activities in this country. This Bill could have very serious repercussions on our cultural communities and industries. They are struggling to survive against very difficult odds caused by nations that have much larger markets and, therefore, greater capacity to be competitive.
The Bill has no provision to offset a high deficit, into the billions, in the trade of technology-intensive products. It does not make provision for the development of high-tech industries
and the protection of fledgling new industries emerging in Canada. Their opportunities may be squeezed considerably or wiped out if a Bill of this nature becomes law without any consideration for the interest of this new high technology industry. In total, that industry is doing badly when we look at the trade figures and the deficit that we have accumulated year over year.
I have gone through this Bill with a fine-toothed comb on a couple of occasions. Another matter that I find surprising is that there is no provision to trigger Canadian savings into Canadian investment. We have a high percentage of savings in our economy because Canadians are thrifty. The savings do not find their way into the type of investment in Canada that this Bill wants to achieve. Where are the provisions to trigger Canadian savings in this Bill which purports in Clause 2 to encourage investment in Canada by Canadians? If that is to be part of the purpose of the Bill, there should be an arsenal of initiatives to give momentum to our own potential rather than develop an imbalanced kind of approach oriented toward attracting capital and initiatives from outside our borders.
I am puzzled because there is no provision for tax incentives for Canadians to invest in Canada.
Of course not.

You would expect there to be tax incentives. If the Hon. Member feels I am wrong in that, he can correct me at the end of my intervention and tell me which clause provides tax incentives.
Another puzzling aspect is that the Bill is put forward in isolation as to the future of our Crown corporations and their role in an investment strategy for Canada. What will be the role of existing Crown corporations? They are surrounded by uncertainty because of initiatives taken by the same Minister. If he moves ahead with an investment policy for Canada, he will have to indicate what is to be the role of Crown agencies that are owned on behalf of the Canadian people.
Debate on this Bill may not seem to be the proper place for a statement on the environment, but I was hoping that in his speech or in the press releases the Minister would have given an indication as to the environmental guidelines to be followed in connection with the signals going out from this ill-conceived Bill. There could have been some kind of warning or signal to foreign industrial investors that this Bill does not mean open season on the environment. That could be concluded by some foreign investors if they look at the abysmal performance of this Government with regard to the environment.
Members will recall the statements made last July and August by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) as to what he would do with regard to acid rain. Our Prime Minister met with the President of the United States and there has been no action on acid rain. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) met with his counterpart and again there has been no action. One could say the same for the present Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier).
December 12, 1984

I submit I am within the terms of reference of this debate when I state that the Government proceeded with a number of cuts which indicates to potential industrial investors that the environment is becoming a second or third consideration in Canada. Otherwise this Government would not have cut the strength of the Canadian Wildlife Service or the National Research Council's environment program. Also it would not have cut a number of research and development initiatives that have to do with renewable resources. Experience has shown that foreign-controlled branch plants in Canada have been characterized by low levels of research and development, limitations on the ability of the branch plants to export and the fact that branch plants as a rule have short and inefficient production runs.
Many branch plants rely too much on imported technology. This has resulted in a lack of capacity in Canada for the kind of innovation which is an important prerequisite to developing products capable of meeting tough competition both worldwide and at home. These are probably the main reasons, coupled with the fact that, by and large, Canadians want control over their industrial and economic destiny, which led the Liberal Government to introduce the Foreign Investment Review Agency. It was a good measure, one that earned a lot of respect on the part of many Canadians.
What I do find disturbing about the Bill that is before us today is that it does not take into account the main concerns that led to the creation of FIRA in the past. It does not take into account that foreign ownership in technologically advanced industries may one day leave Canadians without participation in the most important growth sectors of our economy. The Bill is silent on that matter. That means that we may have very little, if any, participation in future investments in the advanced industries that may be launched and developed in our country.
The Bill does not take into account that a high level of foreign ownership may one day lead to Canada's future being decided behind the closed doors of corporate boardrooms outside of Canada. Is that what we want to have?
Oh, oh!
Hon. Members over there are moaning and groaning. Perhaps they want to participate in this debate and give us the benefit of their answers to these questions.
Read the Bill.
I have read the Bill. That is why I am raising these questions.
Read it.

I am glad to hear these interjections because it tells me that it hurts. Somehow Hon. Members over there do not like to hear what I am saying and that means that some of their sensitivities are being awakened to the reality of fact.
Investment Canada Act
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the Bill does not take into account that Canadians have, over the development of our nation, reached the point where they do really want to have control over their destiny. Canadians no longer wish to be owned by outside interests. This Bill really turns the clock back rather than moving us forward to a more improved position vis-a-vis our own economy. Certainly Canadians do not want to see the development of the country left in the hands of one Minister who will decide when, where and how these investments will be allowed into the country.
This Bill provides no guarantee whatsoever for the destinies of individual workers and their families. It does not protect the livelihood of a worker who may have been employed by a branch plant for 10 or 20 years. We have experienced in Toronto on several occasions a situation in which one day a worker finds that his branch plant is closed because of a decision-
So what?

So what? Who said so what? I would like to know who said that. That means that there has been a tragedy in the life of a family. It is tragic to lose one's job all of a sudden because somehow, somewhere, in a boardroom across the ocean, a decision was made to close down and one is left without a job. What does one do then? This Bill is silent on this most important social and economic consideration.
I really hope that the Minister will address himself to these shortcomings when the Bill eventually reaches committee stage. There is no answer to the question of what happens to the Canadian worker when a foreign owner decides that Canada's markets have dried up or perhaps that the economy is contracting and it is better to go to another country where the grass is greener.
All of this is in sharp contrast with the promise made by this Government to create jobs. The open-door policy for foreign investors that the Government is announcing will lead to the creation of new business ventures, but will it create jobs? This is the basic question that we would like to have answered. Foreign investment does not necessarily mean the creation of jobs.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are signalling me that my time is up. I thank you for your consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to certain aspects of the legislation respecting investment in Canada, especially those dealing with Canada's cultural heritage and national identity.
We all know, but it is perhaps good to refresh our memories, that new methods being used by the media-including cablevi-sion, pay-television, video-cassettes, personal computers-and by the cultural sector are becoming a focus for industrial, cultural and broadcasting policies. As countries recognize the important economic role of communications in the media and the arts, they have developed increasingly competitive industrial policies in those sectors. There is a growing world demand for cultural products and for new means of communication. This will result, and has already resulted, in an expanding international market for Canadian cultural products and opportunities for Canadians to compete for an increasing share of foreign revenue.
The cultural industries and the performing arts sector can therefore provide Canada with unique opportunities for economic renewal and future economic stability, as expressed in job creation and even trade. We must not forget that the cultural sector of our economy is one of the best ways to address the employment problem, since 60 per cent of each dollar generated is directed towards employment, compared with 20 cents in primary industries.
I believe that increased foreign investment would help us take advantage of and expand these opportunities. However, 1 also believe there is another dimension to foreign investment in Canada's cultural economy. Whether it is reflected in our cultural heritage, in music, films, art or the theater, it is a sector that is a central part of our own national identity. The ability to create, to express and to interpret artistic and social values is, I believe, just as important a measure of a country's
Investment Canada Act
viability. Canada has the advantage of having reached a point in its development where it has several ways of ensuring that this country will be strong both economically and culturally. Investment Canada is an example of this Government's commitment to creating employment and a free and strong industry, while at the same time ensuring that Canada's unique cultural identity will be enhanced.
In the past, the lack of directives and policies in the Foreign Investment Review Act to deal with cultural activities had created a climate of confusion and a lack of confidence that was most undesirable. I believe the Government has a responsibility to explain its policies and objectives in this sector, so that foreign investors will understand what Canada as a country hopes to accomplish in the cultural sphere.
That is why the proposed legislation provides that foreign investment in the cultural sector is to receive special attention and consideration. These guidelines would therefore help foreign investors to take advantage of opportunities in the Canadian cultural sector, while recognizing the fact that it is essential for us to preserve and develop our Canadian cultural identity.
Because of the impact of consumption and of the earning power of Canadian cultural products such as films, TV programs, recordings and editing on the cultural and social development of Canada, the profitability of Canada's cultural industries is a determining factor when reviewing proposed foreign investments in Canada. Both our culture and our economy are important sectors.
Film, video, recording and production industries now contribute $5 billion annually to the Canadian economy. In addition, they indirectly account for $4 to $5 billion in the related sectors of marketing and radio-TV broadcasting. A significant share of that economic activity comes from foreign investment firms and the distribution of foreign products on the domestic market. However, we note that the best opportunities with respect to employment and economic growth in sectors of cultural activities are offered by Canadian businesses. Apparently, that is due to the nature of the products distributed.
On the other hand, the economic activity stemming from films, recording and production is linked with copyright ownership. Indeed, if copyrights are foreign-owned, the revenues generated on the Canadian market will leave the country and create jobs abroad.
Thanks to the cultural intitiatives taken by the government in recent years-regulations on the Canadian contents of programming, the activities of the Canadian Film Development Corporation, known as Telefilm Canada, the assistance program for Canadian production development, the deduction program for film and video capital cost depreciation, and the postal grants program-Canadian cultural industries have

December 12, 1984
Investment Canada Act
been through a period of rapid development and growth these past few years.
That situation made it possible for Canada's cultural industries to explore new avenues so as to ensure economic growth and job creation to meet the ever increasing demand for our cultural products in an environment where new communication technologies are the last word.
Movie and record production has grown substantially thanks to new technological developments in films video digital recording and software for personal use. On the other hand, recreational medias such as television, AM and FM radio, pay TV, videocassettes and VCRs have increased the demand for programming. According to recent studies in the United States, by 1988, there will be a $5 billion market for video products alone, in North America. In addition, electronic publication and the use of computers for this purpose create new markets and new opportunities for the publishing industry.
Per capita, Canadians are the largest consumers of cultural products worldwide. Because of this great demand and of the proximity of the United States, the Canadian market will inevitably be invaded by foreign interests as development opportunities occur.
Direct investment in the Canadian cultural industry by foreign interests can bring in certain benefits if these investments contribute to the production and distribution of Canadian cultural products and if there are more joint ventures by Canadian and foreign companies to this end. During the next decade, this investment will be vitally important for Canadians if they want to take advantage of the market which now belongs to foreign multinationals, especially in view of the high cost of new technology, and greater competition thus resulting in more opportunities for us in Canada.
Investment Canada will play a major role in protecting the economic development interests of Canadian cultural industries. The provisions of the Investment Canada Act which deal with business activities related to the Canadian cultural heritage or to our national identity, such as publishing or distribution of books or periodicals and the production and distribution of movies, will create a healthy climate for Canadians to develop strong cultural businesses and will guarantee access to Canadian cultural activities and products. The review activities will allow for an easier assessment on the part of Government authorities of the economic and cultural implications of a proposed commercial activity.
A clear statement of Government policy objectives for the cultural sectors involved will be given to the investor and financial assistance will be provided with due consideration being given to the intentions of applicants as concerns these policies. This will guarantee not only a review of foreign investment opportunities, but also the development by Canada of its own competitive cultural businesses to meet the needs of Canadian artists as well as our cultural objectives.
That is all, Mr. Speaker. I can assure you that this Bill protects our national identity and will allow us to protect Canada's cultural heritage while providing investments which will create jobs. That is the purpose of this Bill.

speechtext: Questions and comments. The Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the Minister. [ Translation]

Reviewing the corporation's situation over the past seven or eight years, we find that the cuts inflicted on the corporation in actual dollars
December 12, 1984

were of the order of $300 million, without the previous Government ever providing the corporation with the means to have the level of administration expected by Parliament.
Indeed, the current president himself was the first to recognize that the corporation's administrative and financial image was not what it ought to be. Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member need not fear for the CBC's future. With this Government, and ever since the Bennett administration under which the original Act was passed, and the Diefenbaker era when a radio and television agency was established separate from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and the days when former Prime Minister Clark appointed the Applebaum-Hebert Commission, and now with Mr. Mulroney, I can assure you that the CBC has a Government that is sensitive to its role and needs.

Mr. Speaker, this is very interesting. I mentioned that the Minister is a fairly good communicator. He is a fairly good communicator on his side. He just mentioned that the former Government had imposed restrictions on the CBC's increased mandate. I read in today's paper that this Minister says there will be even more spending on the French network. This is imposing again a mandate on the CBC after cutting it as extensively as the Government has done.
I asked the Minister a simple question. He said that the previous Government cut back on the CBC. Then he said that if it had not cut back on the CBC years ago, maybe I would have my radio station. Let me remind him that it was from the cut of this Government that I lost my radio station.
My question to him is quite simple. The former Minister of Communications would be acting if I had brought up in the House of Commons that I had lost the only radio station in my riding. What is the Minister's function under the Broadcasting Act? Is there an appeal procedure to the Minister, or do we have to accept the word of Mr. Juneau, who claims that it was on instruction from the Minister of Communication and this Government that he had to make these drastic moves with his chain saw? What is the appeal procedure? Do the people of Canada have any appeal to this Minister? Does he have any function under the Broadcasting Act as it relates to these cuts and possibly getting some of them overturned or reversed?

Member will know that the CBC's annual report has already been tabled in this House, and that the Standing Committee on Communications has every chance of hearing the Corporation's officials if it so wishes. But as the Hon. Member is aware, it is not within my
Investment Canada Act
responsibilities to direct the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation concerning its day-to-day operations, in areas of its own responsibility.
I would also like to tell him that when I was in Montreal, I saw something which all French-speaking citizens inside and outside Quebec have already realized over a number of years, and that is the fact that among French-speaking viewers there is a tendency to switch from certain programs produced by both private or public television networks, to English-speaking or American TV stations.
That fact is evidenced by all the statistics, and it belongs-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:

Is there unanimous consent to let the Minister continue? I hear a no. I am sorry. Order, please. The Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway).

Mr. Speaker, it is a real pleasure for me to have the opportunity to speak in support of Bill C-15, which is the Bill with regard to investment in Canada, otherwise known as Investment Canada. It is a pleasure to speak because this is really the second part of the Government's program for economic recovery in the country. I believe we should all keep that fact in mind at all times. We should all remember why we were elected and sent here. It was mainly for the purpose of getting the country going again and producing some jobs. This particular Bill is aimed at just that.
Traditionally, since World War II the program which governments have followed to get the economy moving again in times of economic recession has been one of government spending to create jobs. Unfortunately, whether we agree or disagree with government spending, that particular option has been foreclosed to this Government and any government acting in the country at the present time. The reason it is foreclosed is that every time anyone suggests that the Government should start spending again we are immediately met with a great howl in the country asking, "What about the deficit?" That deficit really ties the hands of the Government and limits the options available to it.
Members of the Opposition have commented on the deficit regularly since the beginning of this session. They have indicated that the Government should ignore the deficit and deal with the question of jobs. They have been suggesting that the way to do that is through spending and more spending. That is not, of course, the way they attacked the problem during the election campaign. During the election campaign all Parties recognized that there was a problem with the deficit which had to be addressed first.
The Government has approached economic recovery in the country with the deficit as its number one priority. That was in the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) which was announced in the House early in November. The economic statement dealt with trying to limit growth of the deficit to

December 12, 1984
Investment Canada Act
allow us to put our own financial house in order and to restore investor and consumer confidence in the country.
The second part of the economic strategy, Mr. Speaker, is to encourage the growth of capital investment in the country once confidence is restored. Of course, that is what this Bill is all about. It is simply to encourage the growth of capital and capital investment in Canada because that creates jobs. I have not heard any members of the Opposition who criticize this Bill deny that investing capital does not create jobs.
Ideally, we would all like to see that capital limited strictly to Canadian capital but we realize that historically that has not been the case and that that is virtually impossible in this country. Historically, it has taken capital from abroad to develop and build the country.
Unfortunately, as far as risk-taking is concerned, and the investment in risk capital, Canadians are rather timid and have not been prepared to take the risks necessary to create that pool of capital to create those jobs. That was very obvious during the last two or three years when we have been in the throes of this economic recession. We have not had enough Canadian capital to produce the jobs to pull us up by our bootstraps and get Canadians back to work. Therefore, the Government has been faced with an effort to try to stimulate that investment from somewhere other than Canada.
What approach should the Government take? A number of Members in the House and many people in the country believe that the course we should be taking is an unrestricted course of foreign investment. They believe that the Government should take off all the restrictions and allow all types of foreign investment into this country without review.
On the other hand, there are many in the House who have great concerns about unrestricted foreign investment. These concerns which Hon. Members in the Opposition have been raising include concerns such as plant closures, no exports by foreign owned companies, and lack of research and development by foreign owned companies. I believe that these are all reasonable concerns, but in facing the reality of today and the problem of trying to build investment and create jobs, the Government has had to try to find a way to encourage investment in this country which is not taking place through Canadian themselves.
Therefore, I believe that this Bill represents a compromise, an acceptable compromise for those of us who are Canadian economic nationalists. It is a compromise which will allow further investment capital into this country and will allow that investment capital to create the jobs that 1,500,000 Canadians very badly need.
This does not represent an entire dismantling or elimination of the previous legislation but, in fact, it is a modification of the previous legislation. It is interesting to note that the tests by which foreign investment is to be gauged, in this Bill remain virtually the same as they were in the present Act. In fact, there have been two additional tests added. Those are the tests that concern cultural policy and international competitiveness. In that respect, the Bill modifies the present law and, in some respects, actually strengthens the review process.
It is also interesting to compare the effect the proposed legislation would have on the applications of foreign investors that were reviewed under the present legislation in 1983 to what is now the law, particularly with respect to the area of direct acquisition of Canadian assets by foreign investors, which concerns most people. According to the proposed legislation, 91 per cent of the total asset values that were reviewed under the present legislation in 1983 will continue to be reviewed under the proposed legislation. That is not a great modification but one which should encourage more capital to come into this country and thereby create more jobs.
That is part two of the Government's program for economic recovery. It is only the second part of other parts yet to come. One of those parts which I, other Members and most Canadians are looking forward to is the budget that is proposed for next year.
I believe that as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) approaches the development of that budget he should look to three other areas to help us on the road to Canadian economic recovery. The first area concerns the question that was quite properly raised by the Opposition about attracting and encouraging Canadian investment. I believe that we certainly should be looking at some measures not only to attract capital from abroad but also to attract some more Canadian capital into the risk investment area. I believe this can be done through some further tax incentives. We already have tax incentives such as the dividend tax credit, the tax incentives on housing, the tax incentives for the film industry, oil and gas and research and development. Obviously that has not been enough. All of those incentives so far have not been able to attract enough Canadian risk capital to put 1.5 million unemployed people back to work. In developing his budget, the Minister of Finance should consider that area to see what other incentives can be created for Canadians to invest in their country.
One such area, I would suggest to him, is investment in rental apartment buildings and rental apartment development. Prior to the Benson Budget in 1970, there were some tax incentives in our laws that encouraged people to own and build rental apartments. We must put that sort of incentive back into our Income Tax Act so that we can encourage the building of badly needed rental units rather than discourage them as is the case with the present law.
The second area which I believe the Minister should address is the whole question of foreign trade. That is the key to long-term viability, not only of foreign investment in this country but also of domestic investment. During the last few months I toured two industrial plants in my riding. Both of these plants are subsidiaries of multinational foreign companies. One company is IBM. The IBM plant in my riding is the largest IBM facility in this country. The other is Ortho Pharmaceutical, which is a subsidiary of the Johnson and Johnson organization. Each of them employs many thousands of people in my riding. Each of them has a global product
December 12, 1984

mandate and each of them carries on a great deal of research and development in this country. In fact, the IBM plant in my riding, which employs approximately 8,000 people, has a research lab which will employ approximately 1,000 people by the beginning of next year. Two years ago it employed 200 people and it has been growing by leaps and bounds. That is a subsidiary of a multinational company. That is the sort of thing we can do in Canada with foreign investment.
The people at IBM and the people at Ortho Pharmaceutical tell me that what we should be doing is trying to encourage world product mandates for all subsidiaries of multinational companies in Canada. They tell me it is essential for the foreign subsidiaries and they tell me that building and developing the foreign market is also essential for Canadian companies because, as we all know, Canada is a signatory to the GATT agreements. Under those agreements, the substantial tariff barriers that we once had are falling. One of these days very soon there will hardly be a tariff barrier here. It is not just a concern that foreign investors may pick up their assets and go home, it is also a concern that Canadian investors and Canadian companies will not be able to compete domestically unless they start to compete in the foreign market. What we should have is something in the forthcoming budget to encourage the development of foreign trade, not only by foreign investors but also by Canadian investors, and to encourage at the same time the concept of world product mandates.
The third area that I believe should be brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance is the whole question of consumer demand. It is fine to create a pool of investment capital. We need more of it and we know that investment capital will create jobs, but it is not going to create jobs and no one is going to invest unless consumers spend. Somehow we have to get consumers to spend. We know that we will be able to provide a little bit more of that with some of the pension improvements that have been promised in the Speech from the Throne that are coming soon. I believe we should also be approaching this problem from the same point of view that the United States has approached it. The Americans cut personal income taxes a few years ago, which put more purchasing power into the hands of the public. It allowed Americans to spend more and buy more of the products and the services produced in their country. As a result, manufacturers created more investment and put people back to work. That is the way we can help stimulate the economy of Canada. That is the way we can get people back to work again.
In summation, this Bill, as I have indicated, is the second step in a program of government economic recovery. There will be more, and all of them, including this Bill, will put Canadians back to work again and get Canada moving.

speechtext:

Investment Canada Act

The Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart).

Mr. Speaker. I should like to direct a question to the Hon. Member. He said that the bill will provide employment for Canadians but I would like to know at what cost? How will the amendments to the legislation provide jobs for Canadians? I will give you an example. Last evening, on the television program Le Point, a business leader said he was pleased to see that the Prime Minister has opened the door to American financiers but that in 50 years from now Canada will have become the 51st American state. It may be interesting for businessmen, but not for Canadians who need to sure that the America corporations purchasing Canadian companies will not close them down as they have done in the past when the economy slows down. Canadian businesses could become warehouses responsible for the American products. Can the Hon. Member assure us that the bill will give real protection to Canadian workers?

Mr. Speaker, I wish the Hon. Member had been listening when I was speaking because I think he would have heard the answer to his question. A few years ago-a long time ago in this country-foreign investment would move in because we may have had some lower wage rates and we had tariff barriers to protect that investment. The barriers protected those companies so they could sell their products in the Canadian market alone. Unfortunately, that type of a policy has become obsolete. Those tariff barriers are coming down and have been coming down for a number of years. Very shortly they will virtually disappear.
Anyone coming to this country from abroad and looking for an investment opportunity is not going to come to look at the Canadian market alone. There is just not enough of a market here and there is no protection. When an American company or any other foreign company-and I might say we should not be just restricting this to American investors, we have many investors from Asia who are coming here at the moment- comes to this country, it is not only because it is looking at the Canadian market but because it is considering the advantages of having a company here that will allow it to compete in a broader market, particularly the American market. I have had discussions with the Ministry of Industry and Trade in the Province of Ontario. One of its programs is geared to bringing foreign investors to Canada. This Ministry tells me that it is achieving its greatest success in attracting foreign investors from Asia. The reason is that Asians can build plants here, develop and manufacture a product, and sell that product not only in Canada but in the United States without having to worry about the non-tariff barriers and the quota system which the United States has for products manufactured in Asia. The Americans do not have those same non-tariff barriers and quotas for products manufactured in Canada. Therefore, it is very attractive for that kind of foreign investment to

December 12, 1984
Investment Canada Act
come to Canada. That is the reason foreign investors come here. They are not coming here anymore to produce solely for the Canadian market because of our great tariff barriers, which may contract and dry up the market. They are coming here to produce for the world market, and that is the only way they will be attracted to this country.
[ Translation]

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) on a supplementary question.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's remarks confirm that if we want not only the Americans to come here, but also Canada to do business with all the other countries, Canada must be different from the United States, for there are countries in the world which would rather do business with Canada than with the United States.
However, if Canada should become the 51st State of the Union, as the Prime Minister seems to wish, these countries will seek other markets. I suggest, therefore, that the Hon. Member's remarks confirm the fact that the Bill not only does not protect Canadians workers' jobs, but eliminates the factor which some countries found attrative in Canada, namely, it being different from the United States. And now a short question. If you have ever taken part-as a businessman, you have certainly taken part in negotiations or attended conventions-how is it that the Canadian side is always anxious to make concessions or amend legislation? The Prime Minister goes down on his knees before representatives of American financial circles and says: "Canada belongs to you", although he has no assurance that the Americans will change their protectionist policy with regard to Canadian goods. It seems to me that in any negotiation we should keep some sort of trump in our hand.

Mr. Speaker, I wish the Hon. Member would not try to misrepresent what is taking place here. Certainly the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has not gone to the United States to suggest that we become the fifty-first State of the United States. In fact, he went to the United States and said, "We welcome your investment into Canada" in order to create jobs and put 1.5 million Canadians back to work again. Certainly that is a protection for Canadians and for Canadian workers. It is not protection to continue the same course as the Hon. Member and his former Government followed, a course which did not attract any capital to the country, a course which did not create any indigenous Canadian capital, a course which did not create any jobs and therefore left us with 1.5 million people unemployed.
This Bill or this approach will attract some new capital that will create jobs. In that way it will put Canadians back to work
and protect them much better than the former Government protected them in any way, shape or form.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member made specific reference to capital investment creating jobs. If he had a plant in his riding with 100 employees and assets under $5 million which was acquired by an American or European company, what guarantee would there be that that investment in itself would create any new jobs in that plant? What guarantee is there that that would occur?

Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any guarantee that an investment of that sort will create jobs. I must say that I have many businesses of that size in my riding. I have businesses ranging from the one-persons operation up to operations with many thousands of employees.
Of course, the question is: What would be the purpose of a foreign investor buying the variety of company which the Hon. Member suggested? Given the current economic climate, not only in this country but in the world, and given the current state of economic relations, particularly with respect to tariff barriers, no one from a foreign company will invest in this country at all, either by way of investment in a new business or by acquisition, unless there is some benefit to the company. Surely the benefit is to create a larger profit for the company. One cannot create a profit without increased sales. The way to increase sales is to increase business. Generally, by and large, increase in the size of business increases employment.
There is no guarantee that Canadians who invest in particular companies or try to establish their own businesses will create any real benefit. They may disappear within a few weeks. As a business person and as a lawyer, I have seen many of that variety in my time as well. There is no guarantee of anything in the world. We have to create a climate which will stimulate business so that they can invest and create jobs.
